title: AI across the flower business.
name: FiftyFlowers
short: AI customer-service apps in production since January 2026, which replaced a paid writing tool and save about $24,000 a year, alongside AI product imagery, a company knowledge workspace and storefront integrations.
role: AI Solutions Engineer · earlier AI & Process Innovation Associate
problem: An online flower retailer has very different workflows across customer support, marketing, storefront and product data. The challenge is connecting useful AI to each team’s actual information and tools.
contribution: Built and evolved the internal AI platform, the support applications and Chrome extension, the marketing image tools, the company knowledge workspace, storefront integrations and the DIY-kit data migration, from early prototypes in 2025 to production tools in 2026.
groups: Customer service AI

Four support apps, shared case history and a Chrome sidepanel, in production since January 2026. They replaced the paid AI writing tool the team used before, which saves about $24,000 a year. See the Customer service AI case study.
Company Second Brain
Team knowledge around a personal memory, with a chat that chooses which knowledge to read and lists its sources. Two teams’ knowledge is in so far. See the Company Second Brain case study.
Product imagery
Image Studio and Preset Creation for consistent product photos, plus a separate batch photo-preparation tool. See the Image Studio case study.
Content from customer questions

Six months of support conversations classified into customer-question topics and coverage gaps, with a review queue of FAQ and blog drafts built in June 2026. Nothing publishes without a person’s approval.
Storefront
The AI Floral Assistant, rush-order requests and Share Your Flair contest entries. See the AI Floral Assistant and Storefront requests case studies.
DIY kit data migration

Farm spreadsheets matched to store products, with recipes, purchase links and 2,789 arrangement plans written to a test copy of the store and checked against their sources. See the DIY kit migration case study.
Proposal Manager

Implemented supplied wireframes for event planning, flower recipes, presentations and shopping lists. Not launched; work paused when the kit migration took priority. See the Proposal Manager case study.
next: The tools are at different stages: the support apps and the rush-order form are in production, the shopping assistant ships in the store theme behind the company’s A/B test, Share Your Flair processing has handled every 2025 entry, the knowledge workspace is an MVP, and the kit migration is complete on a test copy of the store.
evidence: Scope reflects the reviewed project records. Screens show empty or invented cases; no customer, order, staff or supplier information is displayed.

title: Every booking since 2009, verified and in one place.
name: Create Spaces
status: Dashboard and ChatGPT connection live · daily export being proven
short: The company’s booking history back to 2009, verified to the cent in its own AWS storage, with a dashboard and a read-only ChatGPT connection live behind a company sign-in; every answer ties its figure to the report row it came from. A daily AI export agent is built and being proven run by run.
problem: Sales information lived inside the company’s desktop business system, as reports someone had to run and export by hand. The team wanted the full history in one place and a safe way to ask questions without losing the original numbers.
contribution: Built the export agent and its verification, the storage and alerting on the company’s own AWS account, the dashboard and the read-only ChatGPT connection. An AI agent with its own cloud computer is set to sign in to the business system each morning and export the previous day’s report, so no one’s computer has to be on; every file is checked against the report’s printed totals before it is kept. The first supervised cloud run passed every check, and unattended runs are being confirmed.
groups: No one’s computer required

A hosted AI agent with its own cloud computer is scheduled to sign in to the business system each morning and export the previous day’s Booking Report as Excel. The first supervised run passed every check; unattended runs are being proven.
Every line checked
A report is kept only when its lines add up to the report’s own printed totals to the cent. The full history back to January 2009 was verified the same way.
The company’s own cloud
Storage sits in Create Spaces’ own AWS account, blocked from public access, with health alarms, a spending alert and an activity log.
Ask in your own ChatGPT

Each person connects their own ChatGPT through a read-only connection, switched on in October 2026. The connection returns every figure with the report row it came from and has no way to change the data.
See the business

A dashboard opens on the latest day, then bookings, gross profit and margin by salesperson for the latest day, the last 7 days, the month so far or all saved history, the original Excel rows, and a calendar of every day received.
next: The verified history, the dashboard and the ChatGPT connection are live on the company’s own AWS account, behind a company sign-in. The daily schedule is being proven run by run.
evidence: Screens use invented sample data generated in the report’s exact format, except the calendar of report days, which shows the real coverage and no figures.
decisions: Verify before keeping.
A new report replaces nothing until its rows reconcile with the report’s printed totals. A failure keeps the last good data in place and raises an alert.
Point every answer at its row.
The ChatGPT connection is read-only and returns the Excel row behind each figure, so an answer can be checked against the source.
decisionNote: More than 1,200 automated tests cover the export, verification, dashboard and connection. The dashboard and the ChatGPT connection went live on 1 October 2026; the daily schedule is the remaining rollout step.

title: Hundreds of kit recipes and 2,789 arrangement plans, moved and checked.
name: DIY kit data migration
status: Delivered on a test copy of the store
short: Matched farm spreadsheets to store products and wrote recipes, purchase links and 2,789 arrangement plans onto a test copy of the store, each traced to its source.
problem: DIY flower kits were defined across farm workbooks and a large internal planning workbook. The store’s product system needed the same recipes, purchase links and arrangement plans, without hand entry and without silent changes.
contribution: Built the readers, matchers and writers with source tracking, so every written value traces to the worksheet cell it came from and every worksheet ends with a recorded outcome.
groups: Read the farm books
509 kit entries read from nine farm workbooks, 504 of them usable. Re-reading the full set of 16 farm books takes about 27 seconds whenever the farms send updates.
Match and write
498 entries matched to store products; recipes and purchase links written for 494, with the rest held for a reason recorded beside them.
Arrangements
All 255 planning worksheets have an outcome; 2,789 arrangements on 139 kits were written, each checked against its worksheet.
Nothing silently changed
Every substitution, missing flower or shortfall went into review lists for the merchandising team instead of being guessed.
next: Delivered on a test copy of the store; moving it into the live store is the company’s next step.
evidence: No supplier names, purchase costs or internal pricing are shown.

title: Better systems for building systems.
name: AI Development Platform
status: In my own daily use · deeper integration in development
short: A development suite for AI agents: project management, engineering memory and orchestration.
problem: AI-assisted work can lose context across sessions and scatter decisions across repositories, conversations and tools. Planning and delivery need a shared structure that humans can inspect.
contribution: Built an internal product suite around three responsibilities: managing the work, retaining engineering knowledge and supervising agent assignments. These tools run my own development process and the client pages I share; deeper integration remains in development.
groups: The Record · manage the work

Project management for developers, clients and connected coding agents. Agents update pages through revision-checked commands with exact-retry receipts, over connections that expire after seven days and can be revoked.
Brain · preserve the context
Durable engineering memory for project state, findings, repository maps, workflows and handoffs, navigable as a graph of more than a thousand linked pages.
Jarvis OS · coordinate execution

A supervisor that has handed bounded tasks to visible Claude Code and Codex workers in recorded trials and reports each one’s real final state. Silence is never treated as success, and an offline worker makes the whole loop testable without paid runs.
Where it came from
Three earlier experiments, a repository that acted as an assistant, a planner and executor split, and a session cockpit, decided which ideas were kept.
The working cycle

Plan a bounded milestone, pursue that work, capture questions and evidence, then review the outcome before planning the next scope. Engineering judgment and release accountability stay with the developer.
next: Bring project context and engineering memory into a more unified assistant experience. The complete proposed integration is not presented as a finished autonomous platform.
evidence: Captures cover private client and project names. Prompts, credentials and implementation details are omitted.

Refuse to guess.

title: A company memory, starting with two teams.
name: Company Second Brain
status: MVP · live since July 2026, two of seven team brains filled
short: Team knowledge around each person’s own memory, and a chat that chooses which knowledge to read and lists its sources, with voice and web research.
problem: Company knowledge was spread across apps, documents and people. Each team needed AI that could use the right part of it and show where an answer came from.
contribution: Built the Second Brain workspace: team brains around each person’s memory, the Engineering Brain view of the shared repository that AI coding agents work through, and a chat that routes each question to the knowledge it needs.
groups: Team brains

Each person’s own memory sits at the center with seven team brains around it. Two hold knowledge today: Customer Service, which already powers the production support apps, and Engineering. Marketing is forming and four are still empty.
Answers with their sources
A small router model picks the brains a question needs, readers pull the top pages, and the answer lists the pages it consulted.
A memory that grows
Add a chat export or a PDF (PDF upload is still to be confirmed on the live site), ask it to research a topic with at most two web searches, or run a check-up for stale and contradictory pages.
Engineering Brain

The shared engineering repository as it stood at the end of July 2026, 135 pages and 854 links, appears as a navigable constellation with a reader. The repository has since grown to 261 pages; bringing the view up to date is the next step.
Voice and gestures
Speech in and out, a live spoken conversation, and camera-based hand tracking to turn and zoom the knowledge map.
next: An MVP, live since July 2026. Customer-service knowledge is in production use; the marketing brain is drawn but holds no knowledge yet, four team brains are placeholders, and the engineering view is a beta that still shows its July snapshot.

title: A visual library for social research.
name: AI Media Manager
status: Prototype · post importing still being proven
short: Connected Instagram accounts and their imported posts in one media library, with organisations and roles. A prototype on its third build; importing is not yet dependable.
problem: Social research starts with a usable collection of accounts and posts. The idea was one place where a brand’s own posts, the posts its customers tag it in and what is working in its field can be looked at side by side, before any AI drafting is layered on top.
contribution: This is the third build in the same area, each replacing the last. The first was a drafting tool: choose a platform, read an AI strategy summary and post ideas, and get a draft rewritten to sound natural. The second was a larger planning dashboard with creator outreach, a week planner and post ideas with reasons, which reached a clickable design before its foundations were dependable. The rebuild goes in phases, each checked before the next. Sign-in, organisations and roles were checked locally and live. The Instagram phase is built but not yet signed off: accounts added by their public username, a media library of imported posts, and a sync engine that drives a headless browser, saves each slide and uses a vision model to read each post page and label each saved slide.
groups: Organisations and roles
One sign-in can belong to several organisations. Each has an owner, admins and members, and an invitation stays pending until it is accepted.
Connected accounts
An organisation’s Instagram accounts sit on one page, added by their public username, each with its followers, post count and sync status.
The media library
The account’s own posts in one grid, and a second grid set aside for posts it is tagged in. Opening a post steps through a carousel’s slides with its like and comment counts and caption.
Sync status
Each account shows when it last synced and how long that took, and a sync that crashes or stalls is flagged.
next: Two parts are unfinished. Importing: capturing every slide of a carousel is not yet dependable, a reel is saved as a still picture and not its video, a sync that finishes with gaps is still marked as synced, and bringing in the posts an account is tagged in is not built, because Instagram shows them only after sign-in. And keeping each organisation’s data private to its own members is not finished. Finding what is trending in an account’s field, and AI drafting on top of the library, come after that.
evidence: Every picture on this page is the real interface running on my own machine with an invented brand and sample pictures. The prototype’s only real account data belongs to someone else, so none of it is published.

title: Consistent product photos, on demand.
name: Image Studio
short: Generative product-photo editing with reusable looks: new backgrounds, exact brand colors and transparent cutouts, with the cost of every run shown before it is spent.
problem: A large product catalog needed consistent backgrounds and styles. Editing by hand was slow, and a credit-based third-party tool cost about 15 cents an image.
contribution: Ran the April pilot and its cost case, then built Image Studio and Preset Creation into the company’s AI platform, with usage tracking and team limits, plus a separate catalog-photo pipeline.
groups: A pilot that made the case

Five catalog products on five backgrounds gave 25 image-to-image results: the simplest product kept its shape on every background, while most tight flower close-ups were recomposed. The pilot estimated about 4 cents and 5 seconds an image on the model it tested.
Pick a look
Upload a batch and apply a saved look: background color, vase, lighting, backdrop texture and one of 14 aspect ratios.
Exact color, real cutouts
An exact-color option rewrites background pixels to the brand color after generation; the cutout look produces a transparent PNG.
Looks the team can build
Preset Creation derives a reusable look from example images and a test photo, generates three samples, and keeps up to ten versions.
Costs in view
Every run shows photos times the price the administrators have set and asks for confirmation above 25 cents; administrators see image spend over time and set per-person and team limits.
next: Released in the company platform in August 2026. A full photo-to-result check across every look is the remaining step.
evidence: Pilot images use the company’s public catalog photos. The before-and-after pair is the sample bundled with a built-in look.
decisions: Call the models directly.

The pilot compared a credit-based tool with direct model calls on the same task: about 15 cents against an estimated 4 cents an image on the model tested. The released studio uses a newer, more expensive model, so the saving per image is smaller than the pilot’s estimate.
Show the exact prompt.
Every option writes one sentence of the prompt, and the full prompt is visible before generating, so a look is inspectable rather than magic.
decisionNote: The April pilot also ran 250 text-to-image experiments; they were not scored and are not presented as results.

title: Event flower proposals, built stem by stem.
name: Proposal Manager
status: Built from the team’s wireframes · not launched
short: A web app for floral consultants: an event plan and stem-by-stem recipes become a priced shopping list and a customer presentation. Built, not launched.
problem: A floral consultation produces an event plan: inspiration, colors, flowers and a recipe for every arrangement. The team’s wireframes asked for one place to build it, price it in store packs and give the customer something to keep.
contribution: Implemented the team’s wireframes as a working web app in March 2026: staff sign-in, the proposal editor, catalog search, the recipe-to-shopping-list calculation, and the customer presentation with print-to-PDF and a pre-filled cart link.
groups: The whole proposal in one place
Customer and event, inspiration photos, a color palette, chosen flowers and a recipe for every arrangement. The editor saves as the consultant works, and any proposal can be duplicated.
Flowers from the store catalog
A flower is added by searching the catalog or by asking the embedded AI Floral Assistant, and arrives with its category, pack sizes and prices.
Recipes, stem by stem
Each recipe lists its flowers with the stems per piece and the number of pieces to make. Half stems are allowed, and a recipe can be reused from another proposal.
A calculated shopping list
Stems per piece times pieces, added across recipes, gives each flower’s need. The app suggests the smallest pack that covers it and shows the surplus or shortfall of the others.
What the customer keeps
A presentation of up to 12 pages, from cover and inspiration to recipes and the priced list, printed to PDF from the browser. One button opens a store cart with the chosen packs.
next: Built in March 2026 and not launched; work paused when the DIY kit migration took priority. Before any launch, the presentation page and product search need repairs, and the shopping list needs a line-by-line check.
evidence: Presentation pictures are local renders of the app’s code with an invented proposal; the live presentation page needs a repair. The editor picture is view only.
decisions: Calculate the list, store the choices.
The shopping list is recalculated from the recipes each time it is shown. Only the consultant’s pack choices are saved with the proposal.
Start from the design export.
Five wireframe frames were exported as code on the first day and made interactive the same evening, which gave the team something real to react to.
decisionNote: Built in 74 recorded changes between March 3 and 31, 2026. The shopping-list arithmetic has not yet been checked line by line against real store packs.
nextTitle: Built, with repairs before any launch.

title: Support replies, drafted with the right knowledge.
name: Customer service AI
short: Four AI apps for inquiries, reviews, claims and chargebacks, with shared case history and a Chrome sidepanel. They replaced the paid AI writing tool the team used before, saving about $24,000 a year.
problem: Support representatives answer very different situations: care questions, public reviews, damage claims and card disputes. Each needs the right policy, voice and numbers, and each case can run over several messages.
contribution: Built the four support apps, the shared chat and case history, and a Chrome sidepanel that brings three of the apps (inquiries, reviews and claims) into the support tools the team already uses. Migrated the platform’s serving layer from AWS Lambda to Firebase and Google Cloud.
groups: Four task-focused apps
Inquiry, Reviews, Claims and Chargeback each combine a form with a chosen brand voice, audience and knowledge articles, then produce an editable draft.
Numbers the reply can trust
In the web app, Claims calculates the refund and the store-credit alternative from the damaged products, and the drafted reply quotes those figures exactly.
Knowledge the representative confirms
Articles are matched by keywords and tags and shown before drafting, so the representative sees what the reply will rely on.
One case, start to finish
Input, AI draft, edits, regeneration and follow-ups are saved as one case that can be reopened in its original app.
Where the team works
A Chrome sidepanel recognizes highlighted text on approved support sites and offers the right form, a quick rewrite in the company voice, or a follow-up drafted from the case history.
next: In production since January 2026. The saving comes from retiring the paid AI writing tool the team used before; the figure is my own estimate, not a company or audited number. A number does not cover the rest of the change: replies now start from the team’s own knowledge and voice, refund figures are calculated before a word is written, and every case leaves a history the next person can pick up.
evidence: Screens show invented cases entered for documentation. No customer, order or staff information is displayed.
decisions: Calculate first, then write.
The form computes refunds and credits; the AI is asked to quote those figures, not to work them out.
Keep a case together.
Every step of a case is stored in order, so a later reply starts from what was already said and changed.
decisionNote: Forty user-visible functions were documented across the apps, chat, history, extension and administration.

title: A clearer view of lending decisions.

short: Machine-learning loan scoring inside the lender’s own application workflow, saving about $24,000 a year, with a five-view dashboard for seeing how lending decisions play out.

The savings figure is my own estimate, not an audited number, and it is one part of the value: the dashboard’s five views show the team how scoring, policy settings and lead sources play out across funded loans.

decisions: Protect policy changes from conflicting edits.

Separate observation from simulation.
The analysis distinguishes observed funded outcomes from modeled exclusions. A scenario helps explore a decision; it is not presented as proof that a policy change caused an outcome.

title: Storefront requests, delivered ready to act on.
name: Storefront requests
status: Rush form live · contest processing run on 2025 entries
short: Two storefront flows: rush-order requests that reach support as ready-to-answer tickets, and contest entries turned into review cards and draft store bundles.
problem: Some storefront requests need a person to act: flowers needed sooner than standard delivery, or a couple sharing their event for the yearly contest. Each has to reach the right team complete, with nothing to re-type.
contribution: Built the rush-order form and its request function, from a one-day prototype to the live version. Built the processing step behind the existing Share Your Flair form, ran it over every 2025 entry, then repaired and audited the media.
groups: A rush request in one step
Customers choose event and delivery dates, pick exact products from the live catalog with size and quantity, and add contact details and addresses. The form checks it all before sending.
A ticket in the customer’s voice
Each request becomes one formatted email to the customer-service inbox with the customer as reply-to, so it opens as a helpdesk ticket the team can answer directly.
An acknowledgment right away
The customer immediately sees a thank-you that explains the next step and asks them to stay reachable while farms are contacted.
One entry, two team workflows
The Share Your Flair step turns a saved contest entry into two review cards for marketing and a draft store bundle built from the couple’s photos, story and ordered products.
Every 2025 entry, read back
Every 2025 entry went through it. After a May 2026 repair, a read-only audit found none of the 640 media links broken and every draft photo in place.
next: The rush form has been live since October 2025. Share Your Flair processing has run on every 2025 entry; releasing its media-link fixes and confirming automatic processing of new entries are the next steps.
evidence: The form and entry page are the public storefront pages, shown empty; nothing was typed or sent. The emails are local renders of the real code with invented data.
decisions: Write it as the customer.
The rush email is written in the customer’s voice with the customer as reply-to, so the ticket reads naturally and no helpdesk integration is needed.
Read back every write.
The first run’s writes were all accepted, yet some links were broken and some drafts short of photos. Only re-reading every card proved a clean state.
decisionNote: Neither flow uses an AI model. Both are forms, checks and routing into the tools each team already works in.

title: Broker outreach, being proven one step at a time.
name: SiteSift AI
short: An AI assistant for commercial real-estate advisors, built to email listing brokers, read their replies into the advisor’s tracker and flag the decisions that are hers. In development: the private beta is paused while each step is proven on live test campaigns.
problem: A tenant-representation advisor screens a list of 5 to 30 candidate properties by emailing every listing broker, reading each reply and recording the answers in a tracker. The emails go out under her name, so every message and every recorded figure has to be right.
contribution: Built the product’s engineering: the advisor’s dashboard and campaign wizard, and the email worker that sends an opening per property, reads broker replies and attachments, writes stated facts to the property’s tracker row and drafts replies in the advisor’s voice. The first beta showed that automated email was not yet meeting that standard, so the beta is paused while each step is proven before advisors rely on it again.
groups: Check every row first
The advisor uploads her own spreadsheet. Each property shows the contact and street it will write to before anything is sent, and any row can be left out.
One right opening per broker
One email per property, greeted by first name or not at all, carrying the client’s requirements and a plain way to say the space is gone or to offer another building.
Facts to the right row

Rent, size, power, doors and clear height go to the property’s own row as the broker stated them, including mixed bases such as yearly rent with monthly charges. Figures for other buildings must never be written there.
Attachments read
Flyers, brochures and availability lists are read for the row they belong to, or the advisor is told exactly which file could not be read.
Replies in her voice
Questions the outreach already answers are answered without involving the advisor, a missing fact is asked for once, and a finished conversation is closed with thanks.
Her decisions, clearly flagged
Call requests, alternative buildings and replies that must wait on an owner become cards that say what happened and what was or was not sent, leaving the choice to her.
next: SiteSift is not open to users today. Each of its eight steps has measurable criteria that count only when proven on a live test campaign against the build that is serving: nine of 22 so far, and no step is complete yet. The beta stays paused until every fault a broker could see is closed.
evidence: Screens come from a test account with every address and identity masked. No client correspondence, broker or prospect information is shown.
decisions: Test fixes against the real model.

A harness feeds realistic broker replies through the product’s single reply entry point with the real model, under a dollar cap per run; reading one reply costs about 14 cents. Its first run traced every failure to the rules around the model rather than the model itself.
Pin every known fault.
An offline sweep of 869 realistic phrasings costs nothing to run. Each failing case is pinned to a named fault, so a fix shows up as a flipped test instead of passing silently.
Prove it live with the fewest emails.

Changes are proven on single-property campaigns between owned test mailboxes, with a fixed email and spend budget. One overnight session ran six such campaigns and shipped four releases for $1.55 of model spend.
decisionNote: More than 10,000 automated backend tests and about 3,800 dashboard and cloud-function tests (local runs, 28 September 2026, with 13 known failures tracked by name). Passing tests are not counted as proof here; only live test campaigns are.

title: Flower requests, answered from the catalog.
name: AI Floral Assistant
status: In the store theme · behind an A/B test since January 2026
short: A storefront chat panel: shoppers describe what they need and get matching catalog products with prices. The AI only reads the request; code runs the search.
problem: Shoppers know the event, the colors and the budget, not the product names. The goal was a way to describe a need in plain words and get catalog products back, with no chance of an invented product or price.
contribution: Built the 2025 prototype, then the storefront assistant: the chat panel in the store theme, the conversation and catalog-search functions on AWS, and the prompt that turns a shopper’s words into the store’s own filters.
groups: Ask in plain words
A shopper types what they need. One small AI call reads it as the store’s own filters: colors, flower types, occasion, budget, effort level, season, product type and what to leave out.
Only what the catalog holds
Code searches the catalog with those filters and returns up to six products with catalog prices. The AI never sees products or writes the reply, so it cannot invent either.
Refine without starting over
The request appears as removable chips. Removing one, clearing them all or asking for new recommendations re-runs the search with no AI call.
Never an empty answer
When nothing matches, the search loosens one condition at a time, such as a higher budget or any of the colors instead of all, and tells the shopper what it changed.
Conversations that come back
A shopper can keep up to ten conversations: on any device when signed in, in the same browser as a guest. Each card opens the store’s product page to choose options and buy.
next: In the store theme since January 2026, hidden unless the company’s A/B test shows it. Next: record who the test shows it to, check card prices against product pages, and measure usage and cost.
evidence: The panel is a local render of the store theme’s code, not the live storefront and not a live AI run: the reading of the request was typed in by hand and the three products are invented. The prototype page is shown empty.
decisions: Let the model translate, let code search.
The model only turns words into filters. The search and the reply sentence are code, so every answer can be explained from its filters.
Ask for the complete new state.
Each call sends the current filters and asks for the full updated set, so follow-ups like “also pink” or “make it red instead” need no merge logic.
decisionNote: The prototype’s 42 test requests ran against the catalog before the move to AWS. No usage or cost figures are claimed; none have been measured yet.

title: The AI plays. The numbers decide.
name: AI Arena
short: Three-a-side AI fighters play a bomb-plant mode in a 3D spectator view, while the same simulation runs headless to measure balance across hundreds of matches.
problem: A match between AI fighters has no correct output to test against. The useful question is whether the game is balanced, and that cannot be answered by watching one match.
contribution: Built a deterministic fixed-step simulation, with seeded randomness, a 60 Hz step and physics stepped in a fixed order, that the browser renders and a headless runner batches. Built the fighters' perception, cover, routes, morale and weapon timing.
groups: Spectator view
A 3D scene with an automatic camera director and a match HUD. Any seed can be replayed, paused or fast-forwarded.
Fighter decisions
Perception, cover, routes, morale and weapon timing produce the contest: simulation logic, not chat agents.
Balance laboratory
Headless batches report team wins, the attack and defense split, round outcomes and each fighter’s impact; every shot is logged with its probability factors.
Decisions from data

470 logged matches across three batches. In the final 100 matches, attackers won 44.9% of rounds, inside the balance gate, while one team still took 63% of matches, an edge recorded rather than hidden.
next: Complete as a local build. Two runs of the same seed already produce byte-identical results (checked 1 October 2026); making that a committed test is next.
evidence: Screens are from the local build. Balance figures come from the committed batch logs.
